planting.note: Repot or mount divisions in spring before the brighter, warmer growth period.

directions: Vampire orchid is grown in slatted baskets with coarse bark or sphagnum that stays constantly moist and well aerated. It needs cool night temperatures and high humidity year-round to produce its dark, pendant flowers on tall arching spikes. Shelter it from direct sun and feed lightly, since cloud-forest Dracula species are sensitive to fertilizer salts. Repot or disturb roots only after a spike finishes flowering.
sources: Marie Selby Botanical Gardens Orchid Identification Center

subcategory: submersed aquarium and pond stem plant

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings into substrate once aquarium or pond water has stabilized.

directions: Giant pearl grass is a fast-growing stem plant popular in planted freshwater aquariums and outdoor water gardens for its whorls of small rounded leaves. Under bright light and a nutrient-rich substrate it forms dense, bushy stands that are trimmed regularly to keep a neat shape. It also grows well emersed along pond margins and bog edges with wet feet. New plants are started simply by cutting and replanting healthy stem tips.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into sharply drained, sandy soil.

directions: Plumed featherflower is a wiry Western Australian shrub prized by florists and native-garden growers for its dense clusters of fringed, feathery flowers held above fine needle-like foliage. It demands excellent drainage and resents phosphorus-rich fertilizer, so lean, sandy mixes similar to its native heath country suit it best. Light pruning after flowering keeps growth compact and encourages the next season's bloom. Established plants tolerate drought but struggle in humid, poorly drained gardens.
sources: Kings Park and Botanic Garden (Western Australia)

planting.note: Scatter a handful of starter plants onto still water once it has warmed in spring.

directions: Mosquito fern is a tiny floating fern long used in rice paddies and backyard ponds for its rapid growth and nitrogen-fixing partnership with cyanobacteria. Fronds shift from green to reddish bronze in bright light or cool weather, creating a colorful floating mat. It multiplies quickly by simple division of its branching fronds, so most gardeners thin it regularly to keep it from covering an entire water surface. Hard freezes kill the fronds, though it can regrow from spores the following season in milder climates.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in spring or early fall into well-drained soil.

directions: Cliff green is a low, mat-forming evergreen shrub native to Appalachian limestone outcrops, grown as a tough groundcover for slopes and rock gardens. Its small, glossy, boxwood-like leaves stay attractive through winter and handle drought and shade better than true boxwood. Plants spread slowly by rooting stems, so occasional division or layering is the easiest way to start new patches. It needs little pruning beyond shaping and is rarely troubled by pests or disease.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring once frost danger has passed.

directions: Ngaio is a fast-growing New Zealand coastal tree or large shrub planted in mild climates as a windbreak and seaside hedge for its glossy, resinous foliage and tolerance of salt spray. Small white dotted flowers give way to purplish berries that attract birds. It adapts to poor, sandy soils and needs little irrigation once established, though young plants appreciate supplemental water their first summer. Regular shearing keeps it dense for hedging, while unpruned specimens develop into small, rounded trees.

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizome sections in spring as new shoots begin to emerge.

directions: Kimmei bamboo is a striking running bamboo grown for bright yellow culms randomly striped with green, a sought-after sport of the species used for screening and specimen planting. New culms color up fully only when exposed to good sunlight, so it performs best in open positions rather than deep shade. Like other running bamboos it benefits from a buried barrier or container to control spread in garden settings. Established clumps tolerate clay soils and occasional drought once roots are settled in.

planting.note: Divide clumps or set out container plants in spring once soil has warmed.

directions: Dwarf rock lily is a small New Zealand grass-like perennial grown for slender foliage that is often flushed bronze or purple, forming neat tufts in rockeries and container plantings. Dainty white star-shaped flowers appear on thin wiry stems above the leaves in late spring. It prefers light, free-draining soil and some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun, especially in warmer climates. Clumps can be lifted and divided every few years to refresh plantings and produce new starts.

planting.note: Set out transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Orange-eyed night phlox is a low, spreading South African perennial that forms a tight mat of narrow leaves studded with small white flowers marked by a vivid orange-red center. Like its taller relatives, the blooms release a stronger fragrance in the evening to attract night-flying pollinators. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil and full sun, tolerating heat and drought once established. Shearing lightly after the main flush of bloom encourages repeat flowering through the warm season.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in early spring or late summer into a prepared seedbed for pasture or meadow mixes.

directions: Yellow oat-grass is a European perennial grass valued in hay meadows and pasture mixes for its early growth and attractive golden flower heads at maturity. It establishes readily from seed and tolerates a range of soils, performing best on fertile, well-drained ground. Growers typically include it as one component of a diverse meadow or forage seed mix rather than sowing it alone. Regular grazing or an annual hay cut keeps stands productive and prevents the growth from becoming overly fibrous.
sources: Emorsgate Wild Seeds (UK native seed supplier)

planting.note: Divide and pot clumps in spring as new growth begins.

directions: Yellow nun's orchid is a terrestrial, pleated-leaved orchid grown in shaded garden beds and pots across the subtropics for its upright spikes of soft yellow flowers. It prefers humus-rich, well-drained soil kept evenly moist during active growth and a drier rest once flowering finishes. Established clumps multiply readily and benefit from division every few years to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding. Protection from direct midday sun and frost keeps the foliage from scorching or browning.

planting.note: Broadcast seed on prepared soil in early spring or fall for roadside or saline-soil plantings.

directions: Weeping alkaligrass is a tough, salt-tolerant perennial grass used for turf and erosion control on soils affected by road salt or natural alkalinity, where typical lawn grasses struggle. It forms a fine-textured, spreading sod from seed and withstands both wet, poorly drained sites and periodic drought. Conservation and roadside plantings rely on it where few other turf grasses persist. Mowing is tolerated well, making it suitable for low-maintenance utility turf as well as naturalized reclamation sites.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Fact Sheet

planting.note: Pot seedlings or offsets into fast-draining cactus mix in spring.

directions: This old man cactus is a slow-growing, densely hairy columnar species from the high Andes, prized by collectors for the long white wool covering its ribs and partially hiding its spines. It needs gritty, mineral soil with excellent drainage and should stay nearly dry through winter to prevent rot, reflecting its native high-altitude habitat. Bright light and some direct sun keep the wool dense and white rather than sparse and gray. Outside truly arid, frost-free climates it is best grown as a container plant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring, spacing to let the mat knit together by midsummer.

directions: Blue star creeper forms a dense, mossy mat of tiny rounded leaves studded with pale blue star-shaped flowers through spring and summer, making it a popular choice between stepping stones and as a small-area lawn substitute. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and spreads readily by rooting along its creeping stems. Consistent moisture keeps the mat lush, though established plantings handle brief dry spells. Dividing rooted sections is the simplest way to start new patches elsewhere in the garden.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after frost danger has passed into well-drained desert soil.

directions: Paperflower is a drought-tough desert subshrub covered through much of the year with clusters of papery yellow daisy-like flowers that fade to a bleached straw color but persist on the plant rather than dropping. It needs sharp drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, making it a staple of low-water landscaping in the American Southwest. Shearing lightly after a heavy bloom cycle keeps plants tidy and encourages fresh flushes of flowers. It self-sows modestly in favorable sites but rarely becomes weedy.

planting.note: Set out transplants after frost once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: 'Joey' is a compact selection of mulla mulla bred for bedding and container use, valued for its dense, fuzzy pink flower spikes held above silvery-green foliage. It blooms continuously through hot weather and needs very little water once established, reflecting its origins among drought-adapted Australian wildflowers. Good drainage is essential, since it struggles in soggy or heavy clay soil. Where winters are too cold for it to persist as a perennial, gardeners grow it simply as a warm-season annual bedding plant.

This compact selection forms tidy mounds of felted gray-green leaves topped with clusters of papery white everlasting flowers in midsummer. It spreads gently by rhizome to form a weed-suppressing patch without becoming invasive. Cut spent flower heads for dried arrangements or leave them for winter texture. Good drainage prevents the woolly foliage from rotting in wet winters.

This selection of New Zealand wind grass develops arching, fine-textured foliage that shifts from orange-bronze to deep red through autumn and winter. It self-sows modestly in favorable climates but is easily controlled by shearing spent flower stems in late winter. Full sun and lean soil intensify the coloring, while rich or overly wet ground encourages floppy, less colorful growth. It tolerates light shade but colors less vividly there.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

directions: This long-popular hedging selection bears masses of small, bicolored pink-and-white flowers resembling apple blossoms against glossy evergreen foliage. It tolerates coastal wind and salt spray exceptionally well, making it a staple of seaside gardens in mild-winter regions. Shear lightly right after the main flowering flush to keep hedges dense without sacrificing the following year's bloom. It resents waterlogged soil, so plant on a slight mound in heavier ground.

Native to Mauritius, this fan palm is grown for its striking powdery blue-gray leaves that become more intensely colored as the plant matures and receives full, unfiltered sun. It is slow-growing and salt-tolerant, making it a prized specimen palm in tropical coastal landscapes. Young plants show less blue coloring and are easily mistaken for related Latania species until they age. Protect from any frost and provide excellent drainage to avoid root rot.

This long-grown South African alpine cultivar produces a dense carpet of grassy foliage topped with abundant rounded, bright pink flowers through summer. It needs consistent moisture and sharp drainage simultaneously, so growers often use raised beds, troughs, or pans filled with gritty compost. Keep the corms nearly dry through winter dormancy to prevent rot, especially in wetter climates. It is a mainstay of alpine show benches and rock gardens in the UK.

Royal Dewflower forms a woody-based mound covered in large daisy-like flowers that shade from yellow to deep red at the petal tips. Give it full sun and sharply drained, lean soil, since soggy conditions quickly cause stem rot. Water sparingly through the dry season and let the plant rest once flowering tapers off in early summer. It makes an excellent container specimen or bank cover in mild, dry-summer climates.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) PlantZAfrica

directions: Great Fen-Sedge is a bold, architectural marginal for the edges of ponds and slow streams, with saw-toothed strap leaves that arch outward from dense clumps. Plant divisions in aquatic baskets set at the water's edge so the crown stays just above or at the waterline. Autumn color turns the foliage a warm gold, and the dried spikes stand well into winter for structure. Handle the leaf margins carefully when dividing, since the tiny serrations can cut skin.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI)

directions: Fragrant Bouvardia carries clusters of slender, white, trumpet-shaped flowers that release a strong sweet scent after dark, making it a favorite near patios and windowsills. It prefers bright, filtered light, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and protection from hard frost. Where winters are cold, grow it in a container and bring it indoors before temperatures drop. Pinch young growth to encourage a bushier habit and more bloom clusters.

This compact, warm-growing orchid from the Philippines produces branching sprays of waxy yellow flowers heavily overlaid with red blotches, blooming more than once a year under good light. Unlike many of its larger relatives, it stays small enough for a windowsill or small greenhouse. Mount it on bark or grow it in a basket with coarse, fast-draining media, water freely while roots are active, and let it dry briefly between waterings. Bright light without direct midday sun keeps the foliage from scorching while still encouraging bloom.

Buri Palm is a solitary, feather-leaved palm from coastal Brazil that eventually develops a slender trunk topped by a dense crown of arching, plumose fronds. It is slower growing and more cold-tender than its low, trunkless cousin Allagoptera arenaria, so give it a sheltered, frost-free spot with rich, well-drained soil. Regular water and feeding during the warm season speed its progress toward trunking size. Because nursery supply is limited, specimens are usually sourced as seed or small container plants from palm specialty growers.

This low-growing Ecuadorian relative of the more common seersucker plant forms rosettes of rounded, deeply quilted leaves with a near-black, velvety sheen. It wants warmth, high humidity, and bright but indirect light, since direct sun quickly bleaches the foliage color. Keep the growing medium evenly moist but never waterlogged, and use a chunky, well-aerated mix to avoid rot at the crown. Divide congested clumps in spring to refresh older plants and produce new starts.

Mexican Fence Post Cactus grows in tight clusters of narrow, upright, ribbed stems edged with a continuous line of small spines, making it a classic living screen or property-line planting in dry climates. It roots readily from cut stem sections, which is how most landscape plantings are started. Give it full sun and fast-draining, gritty soil, and water only during active summer growth. Once established it tolerates long dry spells and needs almost no maintenance beyond occasional shaping.

Cane Bluestem is a warm-season bunchgrass valued for its silvery, fluffy seed heads that catch low autumn light and persist into winter. It thrives in lean, rocky, or sandy soils across the southwestern grasslands and needs very little supplemental water once roots are established. Cut clumps back hard in late winter before new growth starts to keep the planting tidy. It combines well with other dryland natives in a mixed grass or wildlife planting.

Silver Brunia is a wiry South African fynbos shrub prized by florists for its tight, button-like clusters of tiny silvery-grey bracts, which hold their color and shape for weeks whether used fresh or dried. In the garden it needs the same conditions as other fynbos plants: sharp drainage, low fertility, and no phosphorus-rich fertilizer, which can kill it outright. Full sun and good air movement help prevent fungal problems in humid climates. Established plants tolerate drought well but resent being transplanted once mature.

scientific_name: Paronychia kapela subsp. serpyllifolia 'Creme de la Creme'
directions: Silver Nailwort forms a dense, evergreen mat of tiny silvery leaves that take on peachy-orange tones in cool weather, making it a dependable filler between flagstones or in a rock garden. It needs sharp drainage above all else; soggy winter soil is its main enemy. Once settled, it shrugs off drought and heat with no extra care. Shear lightly after bloom if the mat starts to mound up, to keep it tight and groundcover-flat.

Scarlet Pimpernel is a low, sprawling heirloom wildflower with tiny star-shaped flowers that famously close up before rain or at dusk, earning it the old nickname 'poor man's weather glass.' It thrives in ordinary, even poor soil and needs little attention once seedlings are established. Use it as a charming filler along path edges, in gravel gardens, or scattered through a cottage-style bed. It reseeds freely, so it is best sited where a bit of spreading each year is welcome.

Lo-Mound Sand Myrtle is a dwarf, trailing selection of sand myrtle that stays low and wide rather than mounding upright like the species, making it useful as a woody groundcover on sunny, sandy slopes. Tiny glossy evergreen leaves are joined in late spring by clusters of small white to pink buds that open into star-shaped flowers favored by small pollinators. It needs acidic, humus-poor, sharply drained soil much like its heath-family relatives, and resents heavy clay or standing water. Light shearing after bloom keeps the trailing habit tidy without removing next year's flower buds.

Willow-leaved crowea is a compact, aromatic shrub from the sandstone woodlands around Sydney, Australia, prized for its long and unusually continuous display of five-petaled, waxy pink star flowers held above narrow, willow-like leaves. It flowers most heavily in cooler months but can produce scattered blooms through most of the year in a mild climate. Give it sharply drained, slightly acidic soil and avoid phosphorus-rich fertilizers, which this and many other Australian natives tolerate poorly. Light pruning after the main flowering flush keeps the plant compact and encourages fresh flowering wood.

Sweet plum is a fine-textured, small-leaved evergreen shrub from southern China and Southeast Asia that has become one of the most widely trained subjects in tropical bonsai, prized for its flaky, mottled bark and tolerance of hard pruning. Tiny cream flowers and small dark berries appear on mature wood, though the plant is grown primarily for its refined branching and foliage rather than for bloom. It needs bright light, regular watering, and protection from frost, thriving outdoors year-round only in warm climates and otherwise wintering indoors near a sunny window. Frequent pinching and wiring while young establishes the dense ramification that makes this species such a popular bonsai choice.

Macarthur Palm is a fast-growing, clustering feather palm native to New Guinea and northern Queensland, producing multiple slender trunks from a single base that together form a dense, bamboo-like clump of arching, deep-green fronds. Small cream flowers and later bright orange-red fruit appear in drooping clusters below the crownshafts throughout the year in warm climates. It tolerates a wide range of light from full sun to fairly deep shade, making it one of the most versatile clumping palms for South Florida, Hawaiian, and Gulf Coast landscapes, and it is commonly used as a privacy screen or specimen clump near pools and patios. Keep soil consistently moist and fertilize with a palm-specific blend to avoid the potassium and magnesium deficiencies common to the genus.

Cape cat's tail is a South African winter-growing bulb from the fynbos and renosterveld of the Western Cape, sending up a low fan of strap-shaped leaves in autumn followed by dense, tapering spikes of small bright yellow star flowers in late winter and spring. Like many Cape bulbs it grows and flowers through the cool, wet winter months and then needs a completely dry, sunbaked summer dormancy to reset for the next season, making it best suited to Mediterranean-climate gardens or pots that can be kept dry in summer. Plant in sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun, and water only during the active winter growth period. It is a reliable choice for a winter bulb frame or rock garden alongside other South African species.

'Alba' is the pure white-flowered selection of Spanish hyacinth, a small, shade-tolerant bulb from the Pyrenees that bears loose, one-sided racemes of nodding, bell-shaped flowers on slender six-to-eight-inch stems in late spring. It shares the species' valuable ability to bloom well in the dappled shade under deciduous trees, a position where most small spring bulbs perform poorly, and it naturalizes steadily into drifts by offsets over several seasons. Grow it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil, and plant it in generous groups among ferns and hostas where the white flowers show up well against shade foliage. It makes an elegant companion to the blue-flowered species form, extending the color range of a woodland bulb planting.

Halimium lasianthum is a low, spreading Mediterranean shrub closely related to the rock roses, covering itself each late spring in bright golden-yellow, poppy-like flowers that often carry a dark maroon blotch at the base of each petal. Its soft, gray-green, felted foliage and tolerance of poor, dry, stony soil make it a natural fit for sunny banks, gravel gardens, and coastal plantings where richer soil and summer moisture would cause it to decline. It flowers most freely after a light trim once blooming finishes, which also keeps the naturally sprawling habit tidy. Good drainage in winter is essential, since like most Mediterranean shrubs it is far more tolerant of summer drought than of cold, waterlogged soil.

'Lunette' is a golden-yellow-flowered seed strain of the Livingstone daisy, a South African succulent annual grown for its dazzlingly glossy, daisy-form flowers over a low, trailing mat of fleshy, glistening leaves covered in tiny light-catching papillae. Flowers open only in bright sun and close on overcast days and at night, so it performs best in a hot, open position rather than against a shaded wall. It thrives on neglect in lean, gritty, well-drained soil and actually blooms more sparsely if overwatered or over-fertilized. Excellent for edging, rock gardens, hanging baskets, and gravel plantings where its drought tolerance and nonstop summer color are put to best use.

Copao is a tree-like columnar cactus from the coastal deserts of northern and central Chile, forming a branching candelabra of gray-green, densely spined stems covered in long, hair-like areole bristles that give older growth a shaggy, silvered appearance. It produces large white to pale pink nocturnal flowers followed by a juicy, edible fruit that is harvested regionally and sold fresh or made into preserves. In cultivation it needs the same gritty, sharply drained mineral soil and bright light that most columnar cacti demand, along with a cool, dry winter rest. Grow it in a large container or a frost-free xeriscape bed, as it has little tolerance for prolonged cold or wet conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Woolly blue stemodia is a trailing, silver-gray groundcover native to the coastal plains and dry grasslands of Texas, the Gulf Coast, and south into Mexico, grown for its densely felted, fuzzy foliage and small, pale lavender-blue flowers produced over a long summer season. The woolly leaf surface reflects intense sun and sheds moisture, giving it excellent heat and drought tolerance once roots are established, and it spreads readily to form a low, weed-suppressing mat. It is widely used in xeriscape and rock gardens, spilling over walls and container edges, and tolerates poor, rocky, or sandy soil far better than rich garden loam. Shear back hard in late winter where it persists as a perennial to renew dense, compact growth for the following season.

Kankakee mallow is a tall, shrubby native perennial once thought restricted to a single rocky island in the Kankakee River of Illinois, though it is now understood to be more widely distributed historically and is propagated and sold through the native plant trade as a garden-worthy prairie and cottage-garden perennial. Large, maplelike leaves support branching stems topped by open spikes of pale pink, hibiscus-like flowers through mid and late summer, attracting bees and other pollinators. It grows well in average garden soil in full sun and is notably more tolerant of ordinary conditions than its rare native habitat would suggest. Scarifying the hard seed coat before sowing improves germination, and established plants often self-sow modestly once happy.

'Ruby Necklace' is a popular trailing selection of the South African succulent Othonna capensis, grown for its slender, bead-like, deep purple-to-burgundy foliage that cascades attractively from hanging baskets, wall pockets, and container edges. Small bright yellow daisy flowers appear intermittently above the foliage, especially in cooler months, adding a cheerful contrast to the dark stems and leaves. It is extremely easy to propagate from stem cuttings, roots readily in a gritty succulent mix, and tolerates considerable neglect once established, needing water only when the soil has dried out completely. Bright light brings out the most intense purple coloring, while lower light produces greener, less vivid foliage.

Heliamphora minor is a smaller-growing sun pitcher from the summit plateaus of Venezuela's Gran Sabana tepuis, forming compact rosettes of narrow, nodding, trumpet-shaped pitchers that collect rainwater and drowned insects rather than relying on strong digestive enzymes. Its more compact size and tolerance of somewhat brighter, cooler conditions than other Heliamphora make it a popular choice for growers building a terrarium or cool greenhouse collection of highland carnivorous plants. Keep it constantly moist in live sphagnum moss and perlite using only distilled, rain, or reverse-osmosis water, since mineral buildup from tap water quickly damages the roots. Small white to pale pink flowers are produced on wiry stalks held above the pitchers.

Cut-leaf daisy is a mat-forming Australian native perennial grown for its finely divided, fern-like foliage and prolific small mauve, pink, or white daisy flowers produced over an unusually long season, often nearly year-round in a mild coastal climate. It spreads steadily by self-layering stems to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover and tolerates a wider range of soil and light conditions than many Australian natives, handling light frost as well as coastal exposure. Trim lightly after flushes of bloom to keep growth compact and encourage continued flowering. It works well spilling over retaining walls, in rockeries, and as edging along garden beds and pathways.

Chamomile sunray is a wiry, aromatic Australian perennial subshrub with fine, needle-like gray-green foliage reminiscent of true chamomile, topped from spring through summer by a long succession of small, papery white everlasting daisies with yellow centers. The dried, straw-textured flowers hold their form and color long after picking, making it a useful everlasting for cutting as well as a reliable garden perennial. It needs lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, declining quickly in humid, poorly drained, or overly fertile ground, and is best treated as a relatively short-lived plant refreshed every few years from cuttings or seed. Light trimming after flowering keeps the mounding habit tidy and encourages fresh growth.

'Alba Plena' is a fully double, pure white heirloom form of dame's rocket, an old cottage-garden favorite grown since at least the sixteenth century for its dense clusters of fragrant, clove-scented flowers borne on tall spring stems. Because the flowers are fully double and sterile, this selection produces no seed and spreads only by division or stem cuttings, unlike the single-flowered species which self-sows aggressively and has become weedy in parts of North America. It prefers moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun and benefits from division every few years to maintain vigor. Its strong evening fragrance and non-invasive habit make it a well-behaved alternative to the common species for gardeners wanting the look of dame's rocket without the seeding concerns.

Japanese tanoak, also called shiia, is a slow-growing evergreen tree related to the true oaks, native to the warm-temperate forests of Japan and valued there for acorns sweet enough to eat roasted with little or no leaching, unlike most true oak acorns. Glossy, leathery evergreen leaves and a dense, rounded crown make it an attractive specimen or screening tree in mild climates, while the edible acorns add a modest food-forest value uncommon among ornamental oak relatives. It prefers moist, acidic, well-drained soil and benefits from some shelter from harsh winter wind in its cooler hardiness range. Growth is slow, particularly in the first several years, so patience and consistent moisture during establishment pay off in a long-lived landscape tree.

Kidneywood, also called palo dulce, is a fine-textured, deciduous shrub-to-small-tree found through the drier scrub and canyon country from the southwestern United States south into central Mexico, closely related to Texas kidneywood but generally growing larger and more tree-like. Dense, upright spikes of small white flowers with a strong honey fragrance appear repeatedly through the warm season, especially after rain, drawing heavy pollinator traffic from native bees and butterflies. The wood has a long history of folk use and as a source of a blue-fluorescing dye extracted from heartwood shavings steeped in water. It thrives on rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun and needs little supplemental water once established, making it a good choice for a xeriscape pollinator planting.

'Roseo-Picta' is the widely sold variegated cultivar of snow bush, selected for leaves that carry an especially vivid mix of white, pink, and deep rose-red splashed across a green base, far showier than the plain green species form. Young growth flushes the brightest pink and white, mellowing somewhat as leaves mature, and overall color intensity increases with brighter light. It is most often grown as a container specimen, a colorful mixed-border accent, or an informal flowering hedge in the warmest zones, since hard frost will kill the top growth and prolonged cold will kill the plant outright. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage the dense, bushy habit and maximum fresh, brightly colored new foliage for which this cultivar is grown.

Biqi is one of the most widely planted Chinese bayberry cultivars in its native range, prized for a dependable, balanced crop of dark red-purple, juicy, sweet-tart fruit in early summer. Grow it on an acidic, fast-draining site in full sun and keep a compatible male tree within range, since this dioecious species will not set fruit alone. Grafted trees begin cropping noticeably sooner than seedling bayberries and mature into a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen that tolerates light shade once established. Avoid heavy feeding and waterlogged ground, both of which quickly stress the shallow, acid-loving root system.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Chinese Bayberry for California
Tropical Fruit Forum — Yangmei (Myrica rubra) cultivar grower discussions

directions: Dongkui, whose name translates roughly to 'Winter Champion,' is grown across a larger commercial acreage in China than any other yangmei cultivar and is prized for unusually large, deep purple-red fruit with high sugar content. The fruit clings well to the branch without dropping, giving growers a wider harvest window than thinner-skinned cultivars. Site it in full sun on strongly acidic, sharply drained soil, and pair it with a male bayberry for pollination since the species is dioecious. Because of its size and vigor, give Dongkui ample room and expect a slow but long-lived evergreen tree once it matures.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Chinese Bayberry for California
Tropical Fruit Forum — Yangmei (Myrica rubra) cultivar grower discussions

directions: Heitan, sold in some catalogs as Black Peak or Black Charcoal bayberry, ripens to a color so deep purple-black it is often mistaken for coal-colored fruit, and growers value it for juicy, sweet-tart flesh with the characteristic yangmei aroma. Like other Chinese bayberries it demands acidic, sharply drained soil and full sun, and resents fertilizer-rich or waterlogged ground. Because it is dioecious, a male tree must be planted within pollinating range for the darkly colored female fruit to form. Give young trees frost protection through their first winters, after which established plants handle the typical cold dips of zone 8-9 well.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Chinese Bayberry for California
Tropical Fruit Forum — Yangmei (Myrica rubra) cultivar grower discussions

directions: Shuijing, marketed in English as Crystal bayberry, is a novelty among yangmei cultivars for ripening to a pale, almost milky-white color with only a faint blush, instead of the deep red or purple-black of typical Chinese bayberry. The flesh is soft, juicy, and mildly sweet with less of the tartness found in red cultivars, making it a conversation-piece addition to a collector's planting. It shares the same cultural needs as other Morella rubra selections: strongly acidic, fast-draining soil, full sun, and a male tree nearby for pollination, since the species is dioecious. Its rarity makes it harder to source than mainstream red cultivars, so expect to order from specialty fruit-tree growers.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Chinese Bayberry for California
Tropical Fruit Forum — Yangmei (Myrica rubra) cultivar grower discussions

directions: Carmine is a goumi selection valued for producing unusually long, large berries compared with other named cultivars like Sweet Scarlet or Red Gem, ripening to a bright red with the characteristic silvery dot pattern of the species. The fruit's tartness and mild astringency fade quickly as it fully ripens, giving a pleasant sweet-tart berry good for fresh eating or preserves. As a nitrogen-fixing member of the Elaeagnus family, it tolerates poor, dry, or sandy soils and even coastal exposure, needing only a sunny to lightly shaded spot to crop heavily. Keep grass and weeds back from the root zone and topdress yearly with compost to support the heavy spring bloom and fruit set.
sources: Cornell Small Farms Program — Elaeagnus multiflora (Goumi) production notes

directions: Box myrtle is a wild-harvested Himalayan relative of the better-known Chinese bayberry, bearing small, bumpy, deep red fruit with a sweet-tart flavor eaten fresh or turned into juice, pickles, and syrup across the hill regions of India and Nepal. It grows naturally on acidic forest slopes and performs best in a similar cool-subtropical, well-drained site with full sun to light shade. Like other bayberries it is dioecious, so both male and female trees are needed within pollinating range for fruit to develop. It remains largely uncultivated commercially and is mostly collected from wild and semi-wild stands, so seed and young plants are only available through a small number of specialty exotic-fruit and ethnobotanical seed suppliers.
sources: Purdue University NewCROP — Myrica/Morella species profiles
